claim: Asymmetric cell divisions in the Arabidopsis stomatal lineage are guided by polarly localized cortical proteins.
source: Asymmetric and self-renewing divisions build and pattern tissues. In the Arabidopsis stomatal lineage, asymmetric cell divisions, guided by polarly localized cortical proteins, generate most cells on the leaf surface.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known feature of the stomatal lineage system.

claim: CONSTITUTIVE TRIPLE RESPONSE1 is a negative regulator of ethylene signaling.
source: In a screen for modulators of cell polarity, we identified CONSTITUTIVE TRIPLE RESPONSE1, a negative regulator of ethylene signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about CTR1 function.

claim: Ethylene and glucose signaling have antagonistic impacts on the self-renewing capacity of stomatal lineage stem cells.
source: We subsequently revealed antagonistic impacts of ethylene and glucose signaling on the self-renewing capacity of stomatal lineage stem cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Developmental information may be encoded in both the spatial and temporal asymmetries of polarity proteins.
source: Quantitative analysis of cell polarity and fate dynamics showed that developmental information may be encoded in both the spatial and temporal asymmetries of polarity proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from quantitative analysis presented in the study.

claim: Tuning the relative proportion of ACDs to SCDs can modulate tissue size and organ composition in response to changes in the external and internal environment.
source: Tuning the relative proportion of ACDs to SCDs can modulate tissue size and organ composition in response to changes in the external and internal environment.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the introduction and supported by cited examples.

claim: Intestinal stem cells in Drosophila melanogaster can resize the intestine in response to food availability by shifting the ratio of ACDs to SCDs.
source: For example, by shifting the ratio of ACDs to SCDs, intestinal stem cells in Drosophila melanogaster can resize the intestine in response to food availability (O'Brien et al., 2011), and in rat brains, stem cells are able to replenish differentiated neurons during stroke recovery (Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Brien et al., 2011.

claim: Stem cells in rat brains are able to replenish differentiated neurons during stroke recovery.
source: For example, by shifting the ratio of ACDs to SCDs, intestinal stem cells in Drosophila melanogaster can resize the intestine in response to food availability (O'Brien et al., 2011), and in rat brains, stem cells are able to replenish differentiated neurons during stroke recovery (Zhang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2004.

claim: Cell polarity can precede a division and dictate division orientation, thereby affecting daughter cell size and fate asymmetries.
source: Cell polarity can precede a division and dictate division orientation, thereby affecting daughter cell size and fate asymmetries, often through differential inheritance of specific materials (Knoblich, 2001; Muroyama and Bergmann, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: When the degree of polarity is not sufficient to ensure differential segregation of proteins to one daughter, it can trigger a developmental switch from ACDs to SCDs.
source: When the degree of polarity is not sufficient to ensure differential segregation of proteins to one daughter, it can trigger a developmental switch from ACDs to SCDs (and subsequent differentiation), as was demonstrated for PAR proteins in Caenorhabditis elegans embryo development (Hubatsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hubatsch et al., 2019.

claim: In Arabidopsis, the stomatal lineage produces two essential cell types: stomatal guard cells and pavement cells.
source: In Arabidopsis, the stomatal lineage produces two essential cell types, stomatal guard cells and pavement cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Stomatal lineages are initiated by ACDs that produce meristemoids and stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs).
source: These lineages are initiated by ACDs that produce meristemoids and stomatal lineage ground cells (SLGCs).
evidence: This is stated as a known feature of stomatal lineage development.

claim: Successive ACDs in either meristemoids (amplifying divisions) or SLGCs (spacing divisions) are self-renewing.
source: Successive ACDs in either meristemoids (amplifying divisions) or SLGCs (spacing divisions) are self-renewing.
evidence: This is stated as a known feature of stomatal lineage development.

claim: Terminal differentiation coincides with the SCD, and subsequent differentiation, of a guard mother cell (GMC) into guard cells.
source: Terminal differentiation coincides with the SCD, and subsequent differentiation, of a guard mother cell (GMC) into guard cells.
evidence: This is stated as a known feature of stomatal lineage development.

claim: Altering the balance of differentiation and self-renewal (approximated by the SCD/ACD ratio) in the stomatal lineage changes the size, cellular composition, and pattern of the epidermis.
source: Altering the balance of differentiation and self-renewal (approximated by the SCD/ACD ratio) in the stomatal lineage changes the size, cellular composition, and pattern of the epidermis (Bergmann and Sack, 2007; Vatén et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bergmann and Sack, 2007 and Vatén et al., 2018.

claim: The epidermis largely determines leaf size.
source: Because the epidermis largely determines leaf size (Gonzalez et al., 2012; Vaseva et al., 2018), SCD/ACD ratio also influences overall leaf properties.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gonzalez et al., 2012 and Vaseva et al., 2018.

claim: SCD/ACD ratio influences overall leaf properties.
source: Because the epidermis largely determines leaf size (Gonzalez et al., 2012; Vaseva et al., 2018), SCD/ACD ratio also influences overall leaf properties.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of the epidermis determining leaf size.

claim: Stomatal lineage divisions are often downstream of systemic and environmental cues.
source: These stomatal lineage divisions are often downstream of systemic and environmental cues (Engineer et al., 2014; Lau et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2017; Schroeder et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Regulating the ability of SLGCs to undergo spacing ACDs contributes to developmental flexibility.
source: For example, a recent analysis of cytokinin hormone signaling showed that regulating the ability of SLGCs to undergo spacing ACDs contributes to developmental flexibility (Vatén et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vatén et al., 2018.

claim: The transcription factor SPEECHLESS (SPCH) initiates ACDs.
source: The transcription factor SPEECHLESS (SPCH) initiates ACDs, and its expression is maintained briefly in both daughter cells, then preferentially lost in the SLGC (MacAlister et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacAlister et al., 2007.

claim: SPCH expression is maintained briefly in both daughter cells after ACD, then preferentially lost in the SLGC.
source: The transcription factor SPEECHLESS (SPCH) initiates ACDs, and its expression is maintained briefly in both daughter cells, then preferentially lost in the SLGC (MacAlister et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacAlister et al., 2007.

claim: Downstream targets of SPCH include 'polarity proteins': BREAKING OF ASYMMETRY IN THE STOMATAL LINEAGE (BASL), BREVIS RADIX-LIKE 2 (BRXL2), and POLAR LOCALIZATION DURING ASYMMETRIC DIVISION AND REDISTRIBUTION (POLAR).
source: Downstream targets of SPCH include 'polarity proteins': BREAKING OF ASYMMETRY IN THE STOMATAL LINEAGE (BASL), BREVIS RADIX-LIKE 2 (BRXL2), and POLAR LOCALIZATION DURING ASYMMETRIC DIVISION AND REDISTRIBUTION (POLAR) (Dong et al., 2009; Lau et al., 2014; Pillitteri et al., 2011; Rowe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Polarity proteins localize to cortical crescents and are required for ensuring the size and fate asymmetries of the ACD.
source: These polarity proteins localize to cortical crescents and are required for ensuring the size and fate asymmetries of the ACD (Dong et al., 2009; Houbaert et al., 2018; Pillitteri et al., 2011; Rowe et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each of the polarity proteins can physically interact with signaling kinases and potentially act as scaffolds to ensure the kinases are active in the appropriate cell types and subcellular locations.
source: Each of these polarity proteins can physically interact with signaling kinases and potentially act as scaffolds to ensure the kinases are active in the appropriate cell types and subcellular locations (Houbaert et al., 2018; Marhava et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The scaffolded kinases include MITOGEN ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASES (MAPKs), Arabidopsis SHAGGY-LIKE kinases (ATSKs), and AGC kinases.
source: The scaffolded kinases include MITOGEN ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASES (MAPKs), Arabidopsis SHAGGY-LIKE kinases (ATSKs), and AGC kinases—all multifunctional kinases capable of mediating both developmental and environmental signals, thus potentially linking cell polarity to flexible and tunable development.
evidence: This is stated as known information about the kinases involved.

claim: MAPKs, ATSKs, and AGC kinases are multifunctional kinases capable of mediating both developmental and environmental signals.
source: The scaffolded kinases include MITOGEN ACTIVATED PROTEIN KINASES (MAPKs), Arabidopsis SHAGGY-LIKE kinases (ATSKs), and AGC kinases—all multifunctional kinases capable of mediating both developmental and environmental signals, thus potentially linking cell polarity to flexible and tunable development.
evidence: This is stated as known information about these kinases.

claim: A mutation in CONSTITUTIVE TRIPLE RESPONSE (CTR1) resulted in overall depolarization of BRXL2.
source: From a genetic screen to identify regulators of cell polarity in the stomatal lineage, we found a mutation in CONSTITUTIVE TRIPLE RESPONSE (CTR1), a core component of the ethylene signaling pathway, that resulted in overall depolarization of BRXL2.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen described in the study.

claim: CTR1 is a core component of the ethylene signaling pathway.
source: From a genetic screen to identify regulators of cell polarity in the stomatal lineage, we found a mutation in CONSTITUTIVE TRIPLE RESPONSE (CTR1), a core component of the ethylene signaling pathway, that resulted in overall depolarization of BRXL2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CTR1 function.

claim: The ctr1G738R mutation is predicted to cause a glycine to arginine substitution at position 738 in the kinase domain.
source: The mutation we found is predicted to cause a glycine to arginine substitution at position 738 in the kinase domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and thus, we will refer to this allele as ctr1G738R.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ctr1G738R shows a strong constitutive ethylene response phenotype at the seedling level.
source: Like the previously reported amorphic allele ctr1-1 (Kieber et al., 1993) and the hypomorphic allele ctr1-btk (Ikeda et al., 2009), ctr1G738R shows a strong constitutive ethylene response phenotype at the seedling level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed in the phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The ctr1G738R mutant displayed a small leaf phenotype in older plants, similar to ctr1-1 and stronger than ctr1-btk.
source: The ctr1G738R mutant also displayed a small leaf phenotype in older plants, similar to ctr1-1 and stronger than ctr1-btk.
evidence: This is observed in the phenotypic analysis of older plants.

claim: The small leaf phenotype in ctr1G738R is consistent with leaf epidermal cells undergoing fewer stem-cell-like ACDs and an overall decreased number of cells in the leaf epidermis.
source: This phenotype is consistent with leaf epidermal cells undergoing fewer stem-cell-like ACDs and an overall decreased number of cells in the leaf epidermis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed phenotype based on known relationships.

claim: ctr1-btk and ctr1-1 also caused different degrees of BRXL2 depolarization.
source: We found that ctr1-btk and ctr1-1 also caused different degrees of BRXL2 depolarization (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is shown in the imaging data in Figure 2A–D.

claim: The F1 progeny of a cross between ctr1G738R pBRXL2::BRXL2-YFP and ctr1-btk displayed an intermediate disruption in BRXL2 polarity.
source: The F1 progeny of a cross between ctr1G738R pBRXL2::BRXL2-YFP and ctr1-btk displayed an intermediate disruption in BRXL2 polarity, as well as an intermediate ethylene response phenotype (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in the genetic analysis in Figure 2E.

claim: pTMM::amiRNA-CTR1 lines did not show a strong ethylene response at the seedling stage.
source: pTMM::amiRNA-CTR1 lines did not show a strong ethylene response at the seedling stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), but did show reduced polarity of BRXL2 in the stomatal lineage (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown in the phenotypic analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: pTMM::amiRNA-CTR1 lines showed reduced polarity of BRXL2 in the stomatal lineage.
source: pTMM::amiRNA-CTR1 lines did not show a strong ethylene response at the seedling stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), but did show reduced polarity of BRXL2 in the stomatal lineage (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown in the imaging data in Figure 2F.

claim: Shoot epidermal-only expression of CTR1 (pATML1::CTR1) was sufficient to rescue the reduced BRXL2 polarity phenotype of ctr1G738R.
source: Additionally, shoot epidermal-only expression of CTR1 (pATML1::CTR1) was sufficient to rescue the reduced BRXL2 polarity phenotype and the small leaf phenotype of ctr1G738R (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I.

claim: Shoot epidermal-only expression of CTR1 (pATML1::CTR1) was sufficient to rescue the small leaf phenotype of ctr1G738R.
source: Additionally, shoot epidermal-only expression of CTR1 (pATML1::CTR1) was sufficient to rescue the reduced BRXL2 polarity phenotype and the small leaf phenotype of ctr1G738R (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I.

claim: The rescue results support a direct role of CTR1 in the epidermis.
source: These rescue results support a direct role of CTR1 in the epidermis and reinforce previous work showing that the epidermis drives organ growth in leaves (Marcotrigiano, 2010; Vaseva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the rescue experiment results.

claim: The epidermis drives organ growth in leaves.
source: These rescue results support a direct role of CTR1 in the epidermis and reinforce previous work showing that the epidermis drives organ growth in leaves (Marcotrigiano, 2010; Vaseva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marcotrigiano, 2010 and Vaseva et al., 2018.

claim: A polar crescent of BRXL2 is visible before asymmetric division.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Rowe et al., 2019), a polar crescent of BRXL2 is visible before asymmetric division (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, top-left panels; Video 1), and after division, this crescent is inherited by the large daughter cell (SLGC).
evidence: This is shown in time-lapse imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 1, and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: After asymmetric division, the BRXL2 crescent is inherited by the large daughter cell (SLGC).
source: Consistent with previous reports (Rowe et al., 2019), a polar crescent of BRXL2 is visible before asymmetric division (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, top-left panels; Video 1), and after division, this crescent is inherited by the large daughter cell (SLGC).
evidence: This is shown in time-lapse imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 1.

claim: BRXL2 persists in the SLGC for more than 8 hr after division.
source: Time lapse, however, revealed two additional features of BRXL2 behavior: first, BRXL2 persists in the SLGC for more than 8 hr after division (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, top-left panels); and second, BRXL2 is still expressed in symmetrically dividing GMCs, but is depolarized in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, top-right panels).
evidence: This is shown in time-lapse imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: BRXL2 is still expressed in symmetrically dividing GMCs, but is depolarized in these cells.
source: Time lapse, however, revealed two additional features of BRXL2 behavior: first, BRXL2 persists in the SLGC for more than 8 hr after division (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, top-left panels); and second, BRXL2 is still expressed in symmetrically dividing GMCs, but is depolarized in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, top-right panels).
evidence: This is shown in time-lapse imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There is a correlation between the degree of BRXL2 polarity and cell identity.
source: These results suggest a correlation between the degree of BRXL2 polarity and cell identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BRXL2 is polarized in ACDs and depolarized in SCDs.

claim: The BRXL2 polarity index (BPI) is defined as the fraction of measurements above the half maximum.
source: The BRXL2 polarity index (BPI) is defined as the fraction of measurements above the half maximum; it represents the fraction of the plasma membrane occupied by BRXL2 and ranges between 0 and 1.
evidence: This is the definition of BPI used in the study.

claim: A BPI close to 0 represents a cell with highly polarized BRXL2, while a BPI of 1 represents a cell with completely depolarized BRXL2.
source: A BPI close to 0 represents a cell with highly polarized BRXL2, while a BPI of 1 represents a cell with completely depolarized BRXL2.
evidence: This is the interpretation of BPI values used in the study.

claim: ctr1G738R cotyledons showed a higher average BPI than Col-0.
source: As expected, ctr1G738R cotyledons showed a higher average BPI than Col-0 (Figure 1E), with fewer cells displaying low BPIs (highly polarized BRXL2).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 1E.

claim: There was no significant difference in crescent size or peak height between Col-0 and ctr1G738R when specifically analyzing the low BPI cells.
source: When we specifically analyzed the low BPI cells, we found no significant difference in crescent size or peak height between Col-0 and ctr1G738R (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D.

claim: Stomatal lineage ACDs in ctr1G738R cotyledons were always preceded by the appearance of polarized BRXL2 in the precursor cell.
source: Through additional time-lapse imaging, we demonstrated that, like ACDs in Col-0, stomatal lineage ACDs in ctr1G738R cotyledons were always preceded by the appearance of polarized BRXL2 in the precursor cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, bottom-left panels; Video 2).
evidence: This is shown in time-lapse imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Video 2.

claim: BRXL2-polarized crescents did not persist as long after ACDs in ctr1G738R compared to Col-0.
source: We had also observed that BRXL2-polarized crescents did not persist as long after ACDs in ctr1G738R compared to Col-0 (Figure 6A), and this reduction of BRXL2 persistence would also result in the appearance of relatively fewer polarized cells when observing BRXL2 polarity at a single timepoint.
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: The SIs of different ctr1 mutants were significantly elevated compared to Col-0.
source: Compared to Col-0, the SIs of different ctr1 mutants were significantly elevated (Figure 3A, B, E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 3E and related figures.

claim: The percentage of amplifying ACDs from ctr1G738R cotyledons was significantly reduced compared to Col-0.
source: Strikingly, the percentage of amplifying ACDs from ctr1G738R cotyledons was significantly reduced, while the percentage of spacing ACDs was similar to Col-0 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is shown in the lineage tracing analysis in Figure 3G.

claim: The percentage of spacing ACDs in ctr1G738R was similar to Col-0.
source: Strikingly, the percentage of amplifying ACDs from ctr1G738R cotyledons was significantly reduced, while the percentage of spacing ACDs was similar to Col-0 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is shown in the lineage tracing analysis in Figure 3G.

claim: Many meristemoids underwent fewer rounds of amplifying ACDs during 48 hr in ctr1G738R compared to Col-0.
source: When individual meristemoids were tracked, we found many underwent fewer rounds of amplifying ACDs during 48 hr in ctr1G738R compared to Col-0 (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is shown in the lineage tracing analysis in Figure 3H.

claim: At 3 dpg, ctr1G738R and Col-0 cotyledons had similar numbers of cells.
source: At 3 dpg, ctr1G738R and Col-0 cotyledons had similar numbers of cells, suggesting a similar level of stomatal entry divisions.
evidence: This is shown in the cell counting analysis.

claim: By 5 dpg, Col-0 had accumulated about 30% more cells than ctr1G738R.
source: However, by 5 dpg, Col-0 had accumulated about 30% more cells than ctr1G738R (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is shown in the cell counting analysis in Figure 3I.

claim: Meristemoids prematurely exit stem-cell divisions in ctr1G738R plants.
source: Together, these results suggest that meristemoids prematurely exit stem-cell divisions in ctr1G738R plants, thereby elevating the SCD/ACD ratio and ultimately generating fewer epidermal cells, a higher SI, and smaller leaves.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of lineage tracing and cell counting.

claim: A 10 μM ACC treatment significantly increased average BPI at 4 dpg relative to mock-treated controls.
source: A 10 μM ACC treatment significantly increased average BPI at 4 dpg and SI at 14 dpg relative to mock-treated controls (Figure 2G, J, Figure 3C, E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 2G, J and Figure 3C, E.

claim: A 10 μM ACC treatment significantly increased SI at 14 dpg relative to mock-treated controls.
source: A 10 μM ACC treatment significantly increased average BPI at 4 dpg and SI at 14 dpg relative to mock-treated controls (Figure 2G, J, Figure 3C, E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 2G, J and Figure 3C, E.

claim: In plants overexpressing EIN3 (EIN3ox), the average BPI and SI were higher than in Col-0.
source: In plants overexpressing EIN3 (EIN3ox) (Chao et al., 1997), the average BPI and SI were higher than the average BPI and SI in Col-0 (Figure 2H, J, Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 2H, J, Figure 3E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A slight decrease of BPI and SI was observed in the ethylene-insensitive mutants ein2-5 and the quadruple mutant ein3eil1ebf1ebf2.
source: Conversely, a slight decrease of BPI and SI was observed in the ethylene-insensitive mutants ein2-5 (Alonso et al., 1999) and the quadruple mutant ein3eil1ebf1ebf2, where EBF (EIN3-binding F-BOX) proteins were eliminated to approximate complete lack of ethylene response (An et al., 2010, Figure 2I, J, Figure 3D, E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 2I, J, Figure 3D, E.

claim: In ein2-5 and ein3eil1ebf1ebf2 mutants, ACC treatment did not affect BRXL2 polarity.
source: In these ethylene-insensitive backgrounds, ACC treatment did not affect BRXL2 polarity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that CTR1 acts via the canonical ethylene signaling pathway to modulate meristemoid division behaviors, regulate stomatal density, and limit leaf growth.
evidence: This is shown in the experiment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CTR1 acts via the canonical ethylene signaling pathway to modulate meristemoid division behaviors, regulate stomatal density, and limit leaf growth.
source: In these ethylene-insensitive backgrounds, ACC treatment did not affect BRXL2 polarity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that CTR1 acts via the canonical ethylene signaling pathway to modulate meristemoid division behaviors, regulate stomatal density, and limit leaf growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ACC response in ethylene-insensitive mutants.

claim: Ethylene signaling disrupts BRXL2 polarity primarily through shifting cell identity from meristemoids (which polarize BRXL2) to GMCs (which do not).
source: These genetic and pharmacological perturbations of ethylene signaling indicate that ethylene signaling disrupts BRXL2 polarity primarily through shifting cell identity from meristemoids (which polarize BRXL2) to GMCs (which do not).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined genetic and pharmacological experiments.

claim: BPI may be an easily scorable proxy for stem-cell potential.
source: These results demonstrate how a systemic signal alters tissue-level development and suggest that BPI may be an easily scorable proxy for stem-cell potential, a phenotype that was tedious and labor-intensive to measure previously (Vatén et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between BPI and division behaviors.

claim: Addition of sucrose to the media resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in average BPI in both ctr1G738R and Col-0 cotyledons.
source: Indeed, addition of sucrose to the media resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in average BPI in both ctr1G738R and Col-0 cotyledons (Figure 4A–D, K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4A–D, K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of glucose, but not fructose, decreased average BPI.
source: Addition of glucose, but not fructose, decreased average BPI (Figure 4E–H, L).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4E–H, L.

claim: The glucose signaling-inactive analog, 3-O-methyl-D-glucose (3-OMG), failed to alter BPI.
source: The glucose signaling-inactive analog, 3-O-methyl-D-glucose (3-OMG) (Cortès et al., 2003), failed to alter BPI (Figure 4I, J, L), suggesting that it is glucose signaling, rather than cellular energy status, that affects stomatal lineage progression.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4I, J, L.

claim: It is glucose signaling, rather than cellular energy status, that affects stomatal lineage progression.
source: The glucose signaling-inactive analog, 3-O-methyl-D-glucose (3-OMG) (Cortès et al., 2003), failed to alter BPI (Figure 4I, J, L), suggesting that it is glucose signaling, rather than cellular energy status, that affects stomatal lineage progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of 3-OMG on BPI.

claim: BASL polarity was significantly enhanced with 2% glucose treatment and reduced with 10 µM ACC treatment.
source: Like BRXL2 polarity, BASL polarity was significantly enhanced with 2% glucose treatment and reduced with 10 µM ACC treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: Glucose and ethylene impact cell polarity in the stomatal lineage more generally.
source: These results suggest that glucose and ethylene impact cell polarity in the stomatal lineage more generally.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both BRXL2 and BASL polarity are affected by glucose and ethylene.

claim: 10 µM ACC can still increase the stomatal index in basl-2, although the degree of increase is less than that in Col-0.
source: 10 µM ACC can still increase the stomatal index in basl-2, although the degree of increase is less than that in Col-0 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Polarity proteins play a minor role in directly mediating ACC response.
source: These results are consistent with polarity proteins playing a minor role in directly mediating ACC response.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ACC can still increase SI in basl-2.

claim: 2% glucose treatment promoted amplifying ACDs in both Col-0 and ctr1G738R.
source: Consistent with its ability to decrease average BPI in treated plants, 2% glucose treatment promoted amplifying ACDs in both Col-0 and ctr1G738R (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in the lineage tracing analysis in Figure 5A.

claim: The SI of ctr1G738R grown in the presence of 2% glucose was shifted back to the wild-type level.
source: Additionally, the SI of ctr1G738R grown in the presence of 2% glucose was shifted back to the wild-type level (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with glucose-antagonizing ethylene signaling and boosting the ability of meristemoids to undergo amplifying ACDs.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both ein2-5 and ein3eil1ebf1ebf2 mutants had significantly reduced BPIs with 2% glucose treatment at 4.5 dpg.
source: Both mutants had significantly reduced BPIs with 2% glucose treatment at 4.5 dpg (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F), suggesting that the influence of glucose in stomatal divisions is independent of the core components of ethylene signaling.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F.

claim: The influence of glucose in stomatal divisions is independent of the core components of ethylene signaling.
source: Both mutants had significantly reduced BPIs with 2% glucose treatment at 4.5 dpg (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F), suggesting that the influence of glucose in stomatal divisions is independent of the core components of ethylene signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glucose still affects BPI in ethylene-insensitive mutants.

claim: When treated with 2% glucose, both hxk1-3 and gin2 mutants exhibited a decrease in average BPI similar to their corresponding wild-type controls.
source: When treated with 2% glucose, both mutants exhibited a decrease in average BPI similar to their corresponding wild-type controls, Col-0 and Ler-0 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–J), suggesting that glucose's regulation in stomatal development is not mediated by HXK1.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–J.

claim: Glucose's regulation in stomatal development is not mediated by HXK1.
source: When treated with 2% glucose, both mutants exhibited a decrease in average BPI similar to their corresponding wild-type controls, Col-0 and Ler-0 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–J), suggesting that glucose's regulation in stomatal development is not mediated by HXK1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glucose still affects BPI in hxk1 mutants.

claim: Despite the presence of AZD-8055, glucose still decreased the average BPI.
source: Despite the presence of AZD-8055, glucose still decreased the average BPI (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Glucose's regulation in stomatal development is not mediated by TOR signaling.
source: Despite the presence of AZD-8055, glucose still decreased the average BPI (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glucose still affects BPI in the presence of TOR inhibitor.

claim: Seedlings grown in low-light conditions showed increased BPIs in their leaves after 48 hr.
source: After 48 hr, seedlings grown in low-light conditions showed increased BPIs in their leaves (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2G–I), indicating fewer ACDs took place.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G–I.

claim: The effect of low (11 μE) light on BPI in the true leaves of Col-0 could be reversed by addition of 2% glucose.
source: We could reverse the effect of low (11 μE) light on BPI in the true leaves of Col-0 by addition of 2% glucose, and this response also occurred in ein3eil1ebf1ebf2 plants (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in the experiment in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Sugar in the leaf provides feedback to coordinate epidermal development with photosynthesis.
source: Together, these results are consistent with sugar in the leaf providing feedback to coordinate epidermal development with photosynthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that low light increases BPI and glucose reverses this effect.

claim: The BRXL2 crescent was significantly less persistent in ctr1G738R than in Col-0.
source: The BRXL2 crescent was significantly less persistent in ctr1G738R than in Col-0 (Figure 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and glucose increased persistence of BRXL2 crescent in both ctr1G738R and Col-0 seedlings (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse analysis in Figure 6A, B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Glucose increased persistence of BRXL2 crescent in both ctr1G738R and Col-0 seedlings.
source: The BRXL2 crescent was significantly less persistent in ctr1G738R than in Col-0 (Figure 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), and glucose increased persistence of BRXL2 crescent in both ctr1G738R and Col-0 seedlings (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6C.

claim: A positive correlation emerges between the persistence of the post-division BRXL2 polarity complex in the SLGC and the self-renewal capacity of the meristemoid.
source: In light of the observation that meristemoids in ctr1G738R underwent fewer amplifying ACDs (Figure 3H) and glucose promoted amplifying ACDs in both Col-0 and ctr1G738R (Figure 5A), a positive correlation emerges between the persistence of the post-division BRXL2 polarity complex in the SLGC and the self-renewal capacity of the meristemoid (the SLGC sister derived from the previous ACD).
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of BRXL2 persistence and division behaviors.

claim: There was no significant change in gSPCH-YFP levels upon treatment with either ACC or glucose.
source: We found no significant change in gSPCH-YFP levels upon treatment with either ACC or glucose (Figure 6F–I).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6F–I.

claim: There were no obvious changes in gSPCH reporter peak intensity, onset of expression, or post-divisional persistence in different treatment conditions.
source: We also examined gSPCH reporter dynamics during ACDs in these different treatment conditions and found no obvious changes in gSPCH reporter peak intensity, onset of expression, or post-divisional persistence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is shown in the time-lapse analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The post-ACD BRXL2 crescent persistence in SLGCs was predictive of sister meristemoid behavior.
source: We found that the post-ACD BRXL2 crescent persistence in SLGCs was predictive of sister meristemoid behavior.
evidence: This is shown in the detailed time-lapse and lineage tracing analysis.

claim: BRXL2 crescents persisted, on average, 2 hr longer when meristemoids underwent amplifying ACDs than when meristemoids divided symmetrically.
source: BRXL2 crescents persisted, on average, 2 hr longer when meristemoids underwent amplifying ACDs than when meristemoids divided symmetrically (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6D, E.

claim: There was no significant difference between persistence in SLGCs that underwent spacing ACDs and those that did not.
source: There was no significant difference between persistence in SLGCs that underwent spacing ACDs and those that did not (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There must be communication between the sister cells resulting from an ACD.
source: Together, these results suggest that there must be communication between the sister cells resulting from an ACD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BRXL2 persistence in SLGCs predicts meristemoid behavior.

claim: Ethylene is considered an 'aging' and a 'stress' hormone.
source: Ethylene is considered an 'aging' and a 'stress' hormone (Iqbal et al., 2017; Schaller, 2012) and regulates many different aspects of plant development, often through its cross-talk with auxin (Muday et al., 2012; Strader et al., 2010; Vaseva et al., 2018; Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Iqbal et al., 2017 and Schaller, 2012.

claim: Ethylene regulates many different aspects of plant development, often through its cross-talk with auxin.
source: Ethylene is considered an 'aging' and a 'stress' hormone (Iqbal et al., 2017; Schaller, 2012) and regulates many different aspects of plant development, often through its cross-talk with auxin (Muday et al., 2012; Strader et al., 2010; Vaseva et al., 2018; Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In both root and leaf epidermal cells, ethylene promotes local auxin biosynthesis.
source: In both root and leaf epidermal cells, for example, ethylene promotes local auxin biosynthesis.
evidence: This is stated as known information about ethylene-auxin interactions.

claim: Elevated auxin levels inhibit cell expansion and regulate plant growth.
source: Elevated auxin levels then inhibit cell expansion and regulate plant growth (Vaseva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vaseva et al., 2018.

claim: Elevated auxin signaling can induce expression of ethylene biosynthesis genes.
source: Elevated auxin signaling can also induce expression of ethylene biosynthesis genes (Abel et al., 1995; Tsuchisaka and Theologis, 2004), creating a feedback loop between these two hormones.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abel et al., 1995 and Tsuchisaka and Theologis, 2004.

claim: Ethylene might regulate stomatal lineage cell divisions through its feedback with auxin.
source: In our case, ethylene might regulate stomatal lineage cell divisions through its feedback with auxin.
evidence: This is speculation based on known ethylene-auxin interactions.

claim: Auxin has been shown to influence cell division and differentiation in the stomatal lineage.
source: Auxin has also been shown to influence cell division and differentiation in the stomatal lineage, but there are some conflicting results, with Le et al., 2014 suggesting that auxin promotes meristemoid ACDs and Balcerowicz et al., 2014 concluding that auxin inhibits ACDs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Le et al., 2014 and Balcerowicz et al., 2014.

claim: Higher levels of ethylene and sugar resulted in opposite effects on BRXL2 persistence and stomatal lineage ACDs.
source: We did pursue the cross-talk between ethylene and sugar signaling, and found that higher levels of each resulted in opposite effects on BRXL2 persistence and stomatal lineage ACDs.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Introduction of 2% glucose to growth media increased the stem-cell-like ACDs, even in ethylene-insensitive mutants.
source: Introduction of 2% glucose to growth media increased the stem-cell-like ACDs, even in ethylene-insensitive mutants, indicating that the epidermis is likely perceiving these signals independently.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental results.

claim: The epidermis is likely perceiving ethylene and glucose signals independently.
source: Introduction of 2% glucose to growth media increased the stem-cell-like ACDs, even in ethylene-insensitive mutants, indicating that the epidermis is likely perceiving these signals independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glucose affects ACDs in ethylene-insensitive mutants.

claim: Glucose and sucrose are the major products of photosynthesis produced in mesophyll cells.
source: Glucose and sucrose are the major products of photosynthesis produced in mesophyll cells, and recent work demonstrates multiple modes of communication between mesophyll and epidermis to coordinate these tissues for optimal growth and gas exchange (Baillie and Fleming, 2020; Dow et al., 2017; Sugano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as known information and supported by citations.

claim: Recent work demonstrates multiple modes of communication between mesophyll and epidermis to coordinate these tissues for optimal growth and gas exchange.
source: Glucose and sucrose are the major products of photosynthesis produced in mesophyll cells, and recent work demonstrates multiple modes of communication between mesophyll and epidermis to coordinate these tissues for optimal growth and gas exchange (Baillie and Fleming, 2020; Dow et al., 2017; Sugano et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baillie and Fleming, 2020; Dow et al., 2017; and Sugano et al., 2010.

claim: It is attractive to consider mesophyll-derived sugar signaling as a way to promote growth and stomatal production.
source: It is attractive to consider mesophyll-derived sugar signaling as a way to promote growth and stomatal production, and future experiments could be designed to trace the source of sugar perceived by the stomatal lineage.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of sugar signals.

claim: Previous work considered the expression of the transcription factor SPCH as the key to modulating stomatal ACDs.
source: Previous work considered the expression of the transcription factor SPCH as the key to modulating stomatal ACDs (Lau et al., 2018; Simmons et al., 2019; Vatén et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: While SPCH is necessary for divisions, neither glucose nor ethylene signaling had a dose-dependent effect on SPCH levels.
source: However, while SPCH is necessary for divisions, neither glucose nor ethylene signaling had a dose-dependent effect on SPCH levels.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental results.

claim: Meristemoids vary in cell size, and ethylene and sugar have opposite effects on cell expansion.
source: On the other hand, meristemoids vary in cell size, and ethylene and sugar have opposite effects on cell expansion.
evidence: This is stated as known information.

claim: Smaller meristemoids undergo fewer rounds of ACDs before committing to terminal differentiation.
source: Thus, one possibility, parallel to the situation in the C. elegans germline, is that smaller meristemoids undergo fewer rounds of ACDs before committing to terminal differentiation.
evidence: This is speculation based on cell size observations.

claim: Signals from the meristemoid to the SLGC rely on the mobile peptide EPIDERMAL PATTERNING FACTOR2 (EPF2).
source: Signals from the meristemoid to the SLGC rely on the mobile peptide EPIDERMAL PATTERNING FACTOR2 (EPF2).
evidence: This is stated as known information.

claim: Perception of EPF2 leads to higher MAPK activity in SLGCs.
source: Perception of EPF2 leads to higher MAPK activity in SLGCs (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: Elevated MAPK activity not only inhibits divisions but also enhances BASL polar localization.
source: Elevated MAPK activity not only inhibits divisions (Bergmann et al., 2004; Lampard et al., 2009) but also enhances BASL polar localization (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: BRXL2 polarity persistence in the SLGC could be a readout of the ACD potential of the sibling meristemoid.
source: Thus, BRXL2 polarity persistence in the SLGC could be a readout of the ACD potential of the sibling meristemoid.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed correlation.

claim: EPF2 secreted by the self-renewing meristemoid is perceived by the neighboring SLGC, stimulating the MAPK signaling pathway in that SLGC.
source: In this scenario, EPF2 secreted by the self-renewing meristemoid is perceived by the neighboring SLGC, stimulating the MAPK signaling pathway in that SLGC.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on known signaling pathways.

claim: Elevated MAPK activity promotes nuclear export and cortical enrichment of BASL.
source: Elevated MAPK activity then promotes nuclear export and cortical enrichment of BASL (Zhang et al., 2015), which in turn sustains BASL and BRXL2 polarity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: When the meristemoid becomes a GMC, EPF2 is no longer produced and MAPK signaling is not activated in the neighboring SLGC.
source: When the meristemoid becomes a GMC, EPF2 is no longer produced and MAPK signaling is not activated in the neighboring SLGC.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: Longer persistence of the polarity domain in the SLGC can also act as the source of a signal.
source: We propose, however, that longer persistence of the polarity domain in the SLGC can also act as the source of a signal.
evidence: This is a proposed alternative model.

claim: BASL and BRXL2 polar crescents precede local cell outgrowth.
source: For example, BASL and BRXL2 polar crescents precede local cell outgrowth (Bringmann and Bergmann, 2017; Mansfield et al., 2018) and differential expansion in the SLGCs could also serve as a division-promoting signal to the meristemoid.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bringmann and Bergmann, 2017 and Mansfield et al., 2018.

claim: Differential expansion in the SLGCs could serve as a division-promoting signal to the meristemoid.
source: For example, BASL and BRXL2 polar crescents precede local cell outgrowth (Bringmann and Bergmann, 2017; Mansfield et al., 2018) and differential expansion in the SLGCs could also serve as a division-promoting signal to the meristemoid.
evidence: This is speculation based on known cell outgrowth patterns.

claim: Polarity proteins BASL, BRX, and POLAR scaffold MAPKs, PAX, and BIN2 kinases, respectively.
source: Polarity proteins BASL, BRX, and POLAR scaffold MAPKs, PAX, and BIN2 kinases, respectively (Houbaert et al., 2018; Marhava et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Scaffolding increases signaling output and creates extensive positive feedback on polarity.
source: In many situations, including these three scaffold/kinase examples, scaffolding increases signaling output and creates extensive positive feedback on polarity (Houbaert et al., 2018; Marhava et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Higher signal accumulation in auxin (MAPK, PAX) or brassinosteroid (BIN2) pathways can lead to the production of mobile signals.
source: Additionally, higher signal accumulation in auxin (MAPK, PAX) or brassinosteroid (BIN2) pathways can also lead to the production of mobile signals, and such signals have been connected to coordination of growth and stomatal lineage progression (Houbaert et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2012; Le et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

source: Additionally, higher signal accumulation in auxin (MAPK, PAX) or brassinosteroid (BIN2) pathways can also lead to the production of mobile signals, and such signals have been connected to coordination of growth and stomatal lineage progression (Houbaert et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2012; Le et al., 2014).
